After a long rally, the score reached deuce and both players needed two more points to win the game.

The crowd held their breath during the thirty-shot rally that decided the final game of the set.

His forehand was so powerful that opponents rarely managed to return it when he hit it to the corner.

stage_2_story.text_en:
It was a hot Saturday afternoon and Moshe was sitting in his favourite armchair in front of the television. His grandson Yoav, who studies tennis at a local club, had come to visit and convinced Moshe to watch the Wimbledon final together.

The match was between two great champions. From the first point, the serving player hit a thundering ace that flew past his opponent before he could even raise his racket. Yoav explained to Moshe: 'Saba, that is called an ace — the other player cannot touch the serve at all.'

In the third game, a long rally began. The two players traded forehand and backhand shots from the baseline, each one trying to force an error. The rally lasted twenty-eight shots before one player finally hit the net and lost the point. The crowd applauded warmly.

The first set was extremely close. Every game seemed to go to deuce — forty-forty — before one player managed to win. Eventually the set reached six games each and went to a tiebreak. Moshe gripped his tea glass tightly as the tiebreak unfolded, shot by shot.

Finally, the champion rushed to the net and finished the point with a crisp volley. He won the tiebreak seven points to five.

Moshe turned to Yoav and said: 'This game is like chess — but with your body.' Yoav laughed and said: 'Exactly, Saba. Next week I will teach you how to serve.'

(c) With a crisp volley at the net
(d) His opponent hit the ball out

questions.question: What did Moshe say about tennis at the end?
options: (a) He said it was too slow and boring
(b) He said it was like chess but with your body
(d) He said the rackets were too heavy
